steps.text: If the child vomits, advise the caregiver to wait 10 minutes before giving more ORS solution. Then start giving the solution again, but more slowly. She should offer the child as much as the child will take, or at least ½ cup ORS solution after each loose stool.

result.question: What are the danger signs in a sick child?
result.questionEn: What are the danger signs in a sick child?

steps.text: Cough for 14 days or more, diarrhoea for 14 days or more, blood in stool, fever for the last 7 days or more, convulsions, not able to drink or eat anything, and vomits everything — all are danger signs, based on the caregiver's report.
Chest indrawing is a sign of severe pneumonia. This child will need oxygen and appropriate medicine for severe pneumonia. Refer a child with chest indrawing.

Unusually sleepy or unconscious. A child who is unusually sleepy is not alert and falls back to sleep after stirring. An unconscious child cannot awaken. There could be many reasons. The child is very sick and needs to go to the health facility urgently to determine the cause and receive appropriate treatment. Refer an unusually sleepy or unconscious child urgently to the nearest health facility.

Cough for 14 days or more. A child who has had cough for 14 days or more has a danger sign. The child may have tuberculosis (TB), asthma, whooping cough, or another problem. The child needs more assessment and treatment at the health facility. Refer a child with cough for 14 days or more.

result.question: I see chest indrawing in a 9 month old with cough.
result.questionEn: I see chest indrawing in a 9 month old with cough.

steps.text: The child might have pneumonia. Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs. Pneumonia can be severe. You identify SEVERE PNEUMONIA by looking for chest indrawing.

Look for chest indrawing when the child breathes IN. Normally when a child breathes IN, the chest and stomach move out together. In a child with chest indrawing, however, the chest below the ribs pulls in instead of moving out; the air does not come in and the chest is not filling with air.

If you see chest indrawing only when the child is crying or feeding, the child does not have chest indrawing. If you are unsure whether the child has chest indrawing, look again. If other community health workers are available, ask what they see.
For chest indrawing to be present, it must be clearly visible and present at every breathing in.
